catalog_quote: 2.2. Lexical and grammatical tones. The tone of a given syllable is determined either lexically or grammatically. Lexical tones are unalterable, such as e.g. ná 'you' (sgl obj) and nà 'him, her'. Each syllable of a lexeme bears its specific tone. All combinations of High and Low tones are theoretically possible in a lexeme: L: tə̀ə 'stomach' LL: ə̀ədì 'knife' LLL: èngèdì 'herder, shepherd' ... LH: ə̀ədí 'bone' LLH: óngòsé [sic] 'sweet' ... H: íin 'you' HH: kándír 'on top' HHH: súngúndí 'nail' ... HL: sóotè 'well' (adverb) ... HLH: kéebàdí 'Zaghawa' HLHL: kúudèkúwà 'I hurt'. Most syllables thus bear their unalterable lexical tone. A number of morphemes effecting grammatical differentiation, however, are tonally neutral. Their tone depends on the overall tonal pattern of the lexeme of which they are part. Prominent amongst these are the personal endings of the verb (cf. 6.6.), the plural …

(2) Deciding source is the standard 1993 reference grammar (only grammar in Glottolog's 4-item descriptive list), reached as page-image excerpts, plus an open 2014 sketch with pitch tracks. The newly downloaded table of contents of Werner 1993 shows the book's entire prosodic apparatus is tonal (ch.2 Tonology §2.1-2.6, §6.3 tone of the verb) with no stress/accent heading, so the unreached pages cannot hold a stress rule. A 2015 open-access paper by the native-speaker phonologist Abeer Bashir states outright 'Midob is a tone language while Arabic is a stress language'. No tone statement of its own beyond following the book's transcription.
